name: Powder blue
lede: Powder blue is a pale, slightly greenish sky blue, and the name is older than the color: it began as a term for powdered smalt, a ground blue glass.

sections.title: Powdered glass
sections.body:
The Oxford English Dictionary, as quoted in the Pigment Compendium, defines *powder blue* as powdered smalt, especially for use in the laundry, with examples running from the mid-seventeenth to the early nineteenth century, some of them evidently as a pigment [1]. Smalt is glass colored with cobalt, ground to a powder, and the compendium lists powder blue among its many trade names, beside Saxon blue, Dutch ultramarine and royal blue [2].

The name came from the grading of the product. Smalt was packed in barrels marked by color grade, the best a deep violet-blue and the cheapest a pale powder blue [3]. The pale grade is the one the color word kept.

sections.title: Light or deep?
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary notes that the term has been used for both a light blue and a deep blue [4]. That is the same split the smalt trade had, deep for the best grade and pale for the cheapest [3]. The swatch here, `powderblue` in CSS, is the pale reading, #B0E0E6 [5]. The xkcd color survey's own "powder blue" is a different, more violet pale blue, #B1D1FC [5].

Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the name in English to 1707, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 has two blocks that this color falls into, 185 and 172 [5]. Its nearest neighbors are [[pale-turquoise]], [[light-blue]] and [[sky-blue]]; deeper relatives of the glass itself are [[cobalt-blue]] and [[royal-blue]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, the color covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 11, within six units of color distance [6]. None are from before 1700 [6]. The earliest is Canaletto's *Warwick Castle* from 1748, where it covers about 28 per cent [6]. The largest share, about 40 per cent, is in Sisley's 1873 *Le chemin de la Machine, Louveciennes* [6]. Six of the 11 are French [6].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so this is a color match and not a pigment test.
